content: Max Planck, whose full name was Max Karl Ernst Ludwig Planck, was born on April 23, 1858, in Kiel, Holstein, Germany, and passed away on October 4, 1947. He was a German physicist widely regarded as the founder of quantum theory, a groundbreaking development that fundamentally altered the understanding of physics in the 20th century. Planck was born into a family with a strong intellectual tradition. His paternal great-grandfather and grandfather were theology professors in Göttingen, his father was a law professor in Kiel and Munich, and his paternal uncle served as a judge. Planck was the sixth child in his family, though two of his siblings were from his father’s first marriage. One of his earliest memories was witnessing the Prussian and Austrian troops marching into Kiel during the Danish-Prussian War of 1864. In 1867, Planck’s family moved to Munich, where he attended the Maximilians Gymnasium. There, he was mentored by Hermann Müller, a mathematician who introduced him to astronomy, mechanics, and mathematics. Müller also taught him the principle of conservation of energy, which left a lasting impression on Planck. He graduated from the gymnasium at the age of 17, marking his first formal engagement with the field of physics. Planck was also musically gifted. He took singing lessons, played the piano, organ, and cello, and even composed songs and operas. Despite his talent in music, he chose to pursue physics. When he began his studies at the University of Munich in 1874, his physics professor, Philipp von Jolly, discouraged him from entering the field, claiming that most discoveries had already been made and only minor gaps remained to be filled. Planck, however, was not deterred, stating that his goal was not to discover new phenomena but to understand the fundamental principles of physics. Under Jolly’s supervision, Planck conducted the only experimental work of his career, studying the diffusion of hydrogen through heated platinum. However, he soon shifted his focus to theoretical physics. In 1877, he spent a year in Berlin studying with prominent physicists Hermann von Helmholtz and Gustav Kirchhoff, as well as the mathematician Karl Weierstrass. Planck found Helmholtz’s lectures slow and error-prone, while Kirchhoff’s were meticulously prepared but monotonous. Despite this, he developed a close friendship with Helmholtz. During this time, Planck engaged in self-study of Rudolf Clausius’s writings, which led him to focus on heat theory. In 1879, Planck defended his dissertation on the second law of thermodynamics, titled On the Second Fundamental Theorem of the Mechanical Theory of Heat. He briefly taught mathematics and physics at his former school in Munich before completing his habilitation thesis in 1880, which dealt with the equilibrium states of isotropic bodies at different temperatures. Planck began his academic career as an unpaid private lecturer in Munich, where he continued his work on heat theory. He independently developed thermodynamic formalisms similar to those of Josiah Willard Gibbs, without being aware of Gibbs’s work. The concept of entropy, as introduced by Clausius, played a central role in Planck’s research. In 1885, he was appointed associate professor of theoretical physics at the University of Kiel. His work on entropy and its applications in physical chemistry included proposing a thermodynamic basis for Svante Arrhenius’s theory of electrolytic dissociation. In 1889, Planck succeeded Gustav Kirchhoff as a professor at the University of Berlin, likely due to Helmholtz’s recommendation. By 1892, he had become a full professor. He declined an offer to take Ludwig Boltzmann’s position in Vienna in 1907, choosing instead to remain in Berlin. In 1909, he delivered the Ernest Kempton Adams Lectures in Theoretical Physics at Columbia University in New York City. Planck retired from his position in Berlin in 1926 and was succeeded by Erwin Schrödinger. Planck’s personal life was marked by both joy and tragedy. In 1887, he married Marie Merck, with whom he had four children: Karl, twins Emma and Grete, and Erwin. After his appointment to Berlin, the family lived in a villa in Berlin-Grunewald, which became a cultural and intellectual hub frequented by notable scientists such as Albert Einstein, Otto Hahn, and Lise Meitner. The family enjoyed performing music together, a tradition that had been established in the home of Helmholtz. However, Planck’s life was also filled with profound losses. His first wife, Marie, died in 1909, possibly from tuberculosis. In 1911, he married his second wife, Marga von Hoesslin, and their son Hermann was born later that year. During World War I, Planck’s eldest son, Karl, was killed in action at Verdun, and his son Erwin was taken prisoner by the French. His daughter Grete died in 1917 during childbirth, and her twin sister, Emma, died two years later in similar circumstances after marrying Grete’s widower. Both granddaughters survived and were named after their mothers. Planck endured these tragedies with remarkable stoicism. In January 1945, Planck’s youngest son, Erwin, was executed by the Volksgerichtshof for his involvement in the failed July 20, 1944, plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler. This loss devastated Planck, leaving him with little will to live. By the end of World War II, Planck, his second wife, and their son Hermann moved to Göttingen, where he died on October 4, 1947. Planck’s scientific achievements were monumental. In 1894, he turned his attention to the problem of black-body radiation, which involved understanding the relationship between the color of light emitted by a heated object and its temperature. Experimental data did not align with existing theoretical models, such as Wien’s law and the Rayleigh-Jeans law. Planck initially proposed a solution based on the principle of elementary disorder, which led to the Wien-Planck law. However, experimental evidence soon contradicted this law, prompting Planck to revise his approach. In 1900, Planck introduced the concept of energy quantization, proposing that electromagnetic energy could only be emitted in discrete units, or quanta, proportional to the frequency of radiation. This assumption, expressed as ( E = hnu ), where ( h ) is Planck’s constant, marked the birth of quantum physics. Although Planck initially viewed this as a mathematical construct rather than a physical reality, his work laid the foundation for quantum mechanics. Albert Einstein later expanded on Planck’s ideas, leading to the development of the photon concept and further advancing quantum theory. Planck was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918 for his discovery of energy quanta. Planck’s later years were marked by his resistance to the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, developed by Niels Bohr, Werner Heisenberg, and others. He hoped that wave mechanics would eventually render quantum theory unnecessary, but this was not the case. Despite his philosophical reservations, Planck’s contributions to quantum theory remain among the most significant in the history of science. Throughout his life, Planck maintained a deep commitment to Christianity, viewing God as an omnipotent, benevolent, and incomprehensible force manifest in the laws of nature. He was tolerant of other religious perspectives and critical of dogmatic church organizations. Planck believed that scientific inquiry required imagination and faith, likening faith to a working hypothesis. Planck received numerous honors and awards, including the Nobel Prize in Physics (1918), the Lorentz Medal (1927), the Copley Medal (1929), and honorary doctorates from several universities. His legacy endures through the Max Planck Society, which was named in his honor in 1948.
